question_text: A student skips lunch. By mid-afternoon, an uncomfortable internal state pushes the student toward the vending machine. After eating a sandwich, the discomfort fades. According to drive theory, what happened after the sandwich?
hint: Drive theory describes what happens to tension once the need behind it is met.
correct_answer_citation: Week 04 · Drive Theory: Tension and Reduction

options.option_text: The drive grew stronger, because the sandwich tasted good
options.option_explanation: A satisfied need does not strengthen the drive. The drive is the discomfort, and eating removed it.

options.option_text: The need was satisfied, so tension fell and the student returned to a more balanced state
options.option_explanation: Correct. An unmet need created a drive. The drive pushed the student toward food, and after the need was satisfied, tension fell and the student returned to a more balanced state.

options.option_text: A bigger gap opened between the current state and the desired state
options.option_explanation: Eating closed the gap rather than widening it. The student moved toward the desired state.

options.option_text: The vending machine created the student's need for food
options.option_explanation: Hunger came from inside the student. Marketing can remind people of a need or show how a product reduces the drive, but the need was already there.

question_text: A shopper is considering a paid language-learning app. The shopper is confident that practicing every day will lead to passing a language exam, and really wants a job abroad. But the shopper doubts that passing the exam will actually lead to getting that job. Which belief is weak?
hint: Split the chain into effort → performance and performance → outcome. Which link does the shopper doubt?
correct_answer_citation: Week 04 · Expectancy Theory: Effort, Performance, and Outcome

options.option_explanation: Valence is the value placed on the outcome. The shopper really wants the job abroad, so valence is strong.
Expectancy is the belief that effort will lead to good performance. The shopper is confident that daily practice will lead to passing, so expectancy is strong.
A drive is the uncomfortable state an unmet need creates. The scenario is about beliefs about what happens after acting, which is expectancy theory.
Correct. Instrumentality is the belief that good performance will lead to a desired outcome. The shopper doubts that passing the exam (performance) will lead to the job (outcome).

question_text: A hungry teenager craves one particular brand of spicy ramen but has no money this week. For this teenager right now, what is that ramen?
hint: Demand needs two things behind the want. Which one is missing?

options.option_explanation: The need is hunger, a basic biological requirement. The ramen is the specific product chosen to satisfy it.
Demand is a want supported by both the ability and willingness to pay. The teenager is willing but has no money, so there is no ability to pay.
Correct. The ramen is the specific product chosen to satisfy hunger, which makes it a want. Without the ability to pay, it is not yet demand.

options.option_text: A need that the ramen brand created
options.option_explanation: A marketer can shape a want but cannot create the basic human need underneath it. The hunger existed before the brand.

question_text: A student who is still worried about paying rent signs up for an expensive painting class to grow as an artist. A classmate says, "That makes no sense. Maslow says you have to take care of safety first." Is the classmate right?
hint: Is the hierarchy a strict order of purchases?
correct_answer_citation: Week 04 · Maslow's Hierarchy in Consumer Markets

options.option_text: No. Consumers can pursue several levels at the same time, and the hierarchy is a guide, not a strict shopping sequence
options.option_explanation: Correct. The student is pursuing safety (stability) and self-actualization (growth) at the same time. The hierarchy is a guide, not a strict shopping sequence.

options.option_text: Yes. Higher-order needs can only be pursued after every basic need is fully met
options.option_explanation: This treats the hierarchy as a strict sequence. Consumers can pursue several levels at the same time.

options.option_text: No. A painting class is a safety need, so it sits on the same level as rent
options.option_explanation: Growth and becoming the person one wants to be is self-actualization, not safety.

options.option_text: Yes. A painting class is a physiological need, like food and sleep
options.option_explanation: Physiological needs include food, water, and sleep. A class for growing as an artist serves self-actualization.

question_text: A shopper loves the idea of a rich chocolate cake for the weekend but dreads the calories that come with it. Which motivational conflict is this?
hint: Count the options. Is there one, or two?
correct_answer_citation: Week 04 · Motivational Conflicts: Three Difficult Choices

options.option_explanation: Approach-approach means choosing between two attractive options. Here there is only one option, the cake.
Avoidance-avoidance means every available option has an unwanted consequence. The cake also has an attractive benefit.
Drive reduction is about lowering the tension an unmet need creates. The shopper's problem is one option pulling two ways.
Correct. The same option has both an attractive benefit (the taste) and an unpleasant cost (the calories).

question_text: Two pairs of headphones cost the same. Model A has more features. Model B has fewer, but everyone in the shopper's friend group wears Model B and compliments each other on it. The shopper buys Model B. Which kind of value guided this choice?
hint: The shopper did not choose the one with the most features. What did Model B offer instead?

options.option_explanation: Functional values focus on performance, convenience, and reliability. Model A had more features, so a functional choice would point the other way.
Correct. Social values focus on belonging, recognition, and how others see the consumer. The shopper chose the one that fits in with the friend group.
Experiential values focus on pleasure, excitement, comfort, or meaning. The deciding factor here was the friends, not the listening experience.
That is a motivational conflict, not a value. The question asks what the shopper valued in Model B.
